Yosef had been playing chess online with Jana for four months. She lived in Haifa too, went to the school across the park, and was better at endgames than anyone he knew. When she wrote, "We should play on a real board sometime," his heart jumped.

He almost said yes and fixed a time. Then he remembered his cousin's story about a "friend" who turned out to be someone else entirely.

That evening he told his mother. She didn't forbid it. "Good that you told me. Let's do a video call first, and then we meet in a public place, and I'll be there."

Yosef felt embarrassed. "Ima, I'm fifteen."

"And I'll sit at the next table with my book. If she's who she says, she won't mind."

Jana didn't mind at all. "My dad wants to come too, honestly," she wrote.

On Saturday they played three games at the café by the library. Two parents sat three tables away, pretending to read. Jana won twice.

At the school counsellor's office in Gangtok, Disha sat twisting her dupatta. "It's probably nothing," she said. "I just wanted to check."

For two months she had chatted with Pema on a drawing forum. Pema said she was sixteen, from the other side of town, and loved the same comics. Disha liked her a lot. She'd been curious to meet her for weeks.

Then Pema had written, "Let's meet at the mall on Saturday. Just us. Don't tell your parents, they'll make it weird." And when Disha suggested a video call first, Pema said her camera was broken.

"That's what made me feel strange," Disha said. "If she's a real friend, why the secret?"

The counsellor nodded. "You noticed exactly the right thing. Wanting to meet a friend is normal. Being told to hide it isn't."

With Disha's agreement, the counsellor called her mother during the lunch break. That afternoon, at home, Disha and her mother blocked the account together and reported it to the forum.

qa.q: What reason did Pema give for not doing a video call?
qa.a: Pema said her camera was broken.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling as she sat in the counsellor's office?
qa.a: Disha felt uneasy and unsure, twisting her dupatta, worried that something was wrong with Pema's request.

qa.q: What did Disha do that was wise?
qa.a: Disha stepped back when Pema pushed for secrecy, asked the counsellor, and let her mother be called so they could block and report the account.

qa.q: How does the counsellor see Disha's curiosity?
qa.a: The counsellor sees wanting to meet a friend as normal, but sees the demand for secrecy as the real warning sign.

grounding: It shows a teen curious to meet an online friend who steps back when the friend pushes secrecy, and brings in trusted adults.

passage:
Friday night

I've been sick in my stomach for two days. On Wednesday I saw an offer for cheap game coins: "90% off, today only." I used Mummy's phone payment app while she was bathing, because I knew her PIN. 1,500 rupees. No coins came. The site vanished.

I kept thinking, she'll kill me. She'll never trust me again. So I said nothing. Every time her phone buzzed, my heart jumped.

Today Himani didi found me crying behind the water tank. When I told her, she said, "The longer you wait, the harder it is for the bank to do anything. Tell her now."

So I did, at dinner. My voice shook. I said, "Mummy, I got scammed and I used your money. I'm really sorry."

She went quiet. Then she said, "I'm upset you used my phone. But I'm glad you told me." She called the bank helpline straight away and reported it to the cybercrime number too. We'll change her PIN tomorrow.

I feel lighter than I have in two days.

Divyansh

qa.a: Divyansh lost 1,500 rupees.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling in the two days before telling Mummy?
qa.a: Divyansh felt sick with fear and shame, scared she would never trust Divyansh again.

qa.q: Why was Himani didi's advice important?
qa.a: She pointed out that waiting makes it harder for the bank to act, so telling early could limit the damage.

qa.q: How did Mummy react, and why did it help?
qa.a: Mummy was upset but glad to be told, and called the bank and cybercrime number straight away, which showed that the truth was better than hiding it.

grounding: It shows a teen afraid to tell a parent after being scammed, learning that telling early lets the parent act quickly and limit the damage.

Sharmila, you're getting free gems in that game from someone older? Let your Elizabeth Aunty tell you something from when I was fourteen.

We had chatrooms then. A man in one of them, he said he was a college student, kept sending me things. Music CDs by post. A phone recharge. Then a watch. I felt so grown up. Special.

He always said the same thing: "This is just between us. Your parents won't understand." I didn't tell anyone. The gifts made me feel like I owed him something.

One day he asked me to meet him at the bus depot to "get the next present in person." Something in me went cold.

I showed my mother the letters and the watch that night. She wasn't angry with me at all. She went to the police the next morning, and it turned out he had done this to three other girls.

That's why I'm asking, Sharmila. When a grown-up gives a teenager gifts and asks for secrets, it's never really a gift.

qa.a: Showing her mother the letters and watch that night was key, because a trusted adult could go to the police and stop him.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling an older man who gave her gifts online and asked for secrecy, and explaining why a teen should never accept gifts that come with secrets.

In Class 9, someone in our class chat posted a photo of me from sports day, edited so I had a pig's snout. Then another with my face on a buffalo. I'm Ganga, and I'll never forget the laughing emojis under them. Vikas had made the first one. Others added more.

I felt sick. Hot and exposed, like everyone was staring even when I was alone in my room. My first thought was to make one of Vikas, worse.

I didn't. My cousin had told me what to do once, and I did it: screenshots of everything, with names and times. Then I blocked Vikas and reported the posts on the app. The next morning I went straight to Mrs Joseph, our class teacher, and showed her.

She didn't say "ignore it." She said, "This is not your fault, Ganga. This is bullying." She took the screenshots to the principal that day, and Vikas's parents were called in.

It still stings sometimes. But I didn't become like them.

Lalremsiami came to me before assembly with her phone and a printed sheet. Over the weekend, a group of boys had posted memes in the class chat mocking the way she speaks, with captions in a fake accent, and one edited photo of her face on a cartoon. Pradeep had started it; others joined in.

She spoke very quietly, but her hands were steady. "I didn't reply. I took screenshots, blocked them and reported the posts. My mother said to bring it to you."

I told her clearly that none of this is her fault, and that mocking someone's accent or face is bullying. I thanked her for keeping calm and bringing the evidence.

I took the screenshots to the principal during first period. The boys' parents have been called for tomorrow, and the posts were removed by noon. I have spoken to the class about respect and will check the class chat weekly. I asked Lalremsiami to come to me at once if anything else appears.

Okay, you want to know about the anonymous account? I'm Gargi. It started in February. An account with no photo, called "truthteller_x," sent me messages every night. "Everyone laughs at you." "Nobody wants you in the group." Stuff about my weight.

The worst part wasn't even the words. It was the guessing. I lay awake going through every name. Was it the girls from dance? My old best friend? I even started to suspect Gurleen, who has been nothing but kind to me. I was checking everyone's face at school for clues.

Gurleen noticed I was acting weird and asked. I told her, and I told her I'd suspected her. She wasn't even offended. She said, "Stop guessing. Let's give it to someone who can actually find out."

So we screenshotted every message, reported the account on the app, and that same day I showed my mother and our school counsellor. The account was taken down in a week.

I still don't know who it was. And I've decided I'm okay not knowing.

passage:
Wednesday night

Zubin commented on my dance video in front of the whole class group: "Looks like a cow having a fit." Twenty people laughed. I read it in the bus and my face burned so hot I thought I'd cry right there.

I got home and I was SO angry. I have an old photo of Zubin from Class 7 when he fell in the mud at the picnic. I opened it. I typed a caption. I wanted him to feel exactly what I felt. My thumb was on post.

Then I thought: then it's two people being cruel. And he'll hit back, and it'll go on for weeks, and maybe I'll be the one in trouble.

I deleted it. My hands were still shaking.

Instead I screenshotted his comment and the laughing replies. I showed Mumma. She was quiet, then angry for me. She emailed my class teacher right then, with the screenshots, and said we'll talk to the school tomorrow.

I still want revenge a little. But I'm glad I didn't.

Sunaina

qa.q: What did Zubin comment on the dance video?
qa.a: Zubin commented, "Looks like a cow having a fit."

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when the thumb was on post?
qa.a: Sunaina felt furious and humiliated, wanting Zubin to feel the same hurt.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than revenge, and why?
qa.a: Saving screenshots and showing Mumma worked better, because it stopped the cruelty spiralling and got the school involved.

qa.q: How did Mumma react to the screenshots?
qa.a: Mumma was quiet, then angry on Sunaina's behalf, and emailed the class teacher at once.

grounding: It shows a teen tempted to hit back at a cyberbully with something equally cruel, recognising the impulse and choosing evidence and reporting instead.

He reported the video in the group, and when his friend Suresh asked him to forward it, he said, "No. Delete it." Then he told their class teacher, Shinde sir, before the last period. Thursday night

I have to write this down because I feel awful.

On Tuesday, someone in our group made an edit of Naveen's photo from the class trip, his head on a dancing chicken. I added the music. I thought it was funny. So did everyone. We sent it to the class group.

By Wednesday it was in three other classes. Today Naveen didn't come to school. His best friend said he was crying at home and didn't want to come back.

My first thought was, "It was only for fun. Everyone was doing it." Then I heard how that sounded. It wasn't fun for him.

So I did what I should have done on Tuesday. I deleted it everywhere I'd posted it. I asked the others to delete it too. I messaged Naveen: "I added the music to that edit. It was cruel and I'm sorry. I've deleted it and asked others to." No excuses.

Tomorrow I'm going to tell our class teacher it was us, before she finds out another way.

Farida
